content:
I am using Comparator to check precisely what statement is being proven. In my full proof file, I use import Mathlib but in my challenge file, I was curious what would happen if I minimized imports. To my surprise, I found that I often have to include surprising imports in order for the check to succeed.

As a concrete example, in https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/latest/ComparatorChallenges/HundredTheorems/Theorem87.lean I need to import Mathlib.AlgebraicTopology.SimplexCategory.Basic or else it doesn't work. Here's the full challenge file there:

import Mathlib.AlgebraicTopology.SimplexCategory.Basic
import Mathlib.Analysis.InnerProductSpace.PiL2
import Mathlib.LinearAlgebra.AffineSpace.FiniteDimensional

namespace Theorem87

abbrev Plane : Type := EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2)

def IntersectsIn (A B A' B' P : Plane) : Prop :=
  Collinear ℝ ({A, B, P} : Set Plane) ∧
    Collinear ℝ ({A', B', P} : Set Plane)

def UniqueIntersection (A B A' B' P : Plane) : Prop :=
  IntersectsIn A B A' B' P ∧
    ∀ Q, IntersectsIn A B A' B' Q → Q = P

theorem desargues_plane
    {A B C A' B' C' O Pab Pbc Pca : Plane}
    (hO_AA' : Collinear ℝ ({A, A', O} : Set Plane))
    (hO_BB' : Collinear ℝ ({B, B', O} : Set Plane))
    (hO_CC' : Collinear ℝ ({C, C', O} : Set Plane))
    (hPab : UniqueIntersection A B A' B' Pab)
    (hPbc : UniqueIntersection B C B' C' Pbc)
    (hPca : UniqueIntersection C A C' A' Pca) :
    Collinear ℝ ({Pab, Pbc, Pca} : Set Plane) := by
  sorry

end Theorem87

My LLM tells me that the reason is that SimplexCategory.Basic declares

instance (x : SimplexCategory) : Fintype (ToType x) :=
  inferInstanceAs (Fintype (Fin _))

and then this affects Fintype (Fin 2) in EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin 2).

Of course I can just put import Mathlib in the challenge file, too, if I want this to be "cleaner".

But: is there somewhere I can read and learn about these sorts of issues?

I don't know if this is written anywhere but I encountered this some days ago in my project as well. I noticed it is sensitive to both imports and variable declarations (but if I turn it to a module, apparently it is not sensitive to private imports). I asked some people on discord and apparently it was a known behavior
(offtopic: I am surprised that Desargues's theorem need simplex category)

Weiyi Wang said:

(offtopic: I am surprised that Desargues's theorem need simplex category)

That's literally the topic. I don't want that import, but if I remove that line, it doesn't work.

Oh that's really interesting. I understand the problem now. To repeat what you have in the file so it is more visible to other people:
The single proof file has the blanket import Mathlib and it includes all definitions and theorems
The challenge file contains minimal import for just definition and the statement. In theory it only needs PiL2 and FiniteDimensional, but comparator complains about difference in definition. If one adds the seemingly unrelated SimplexCategory.Basic import to the challenge file, then comparator is fine with it

For my own project I didn't diagnose this deep, but I suspect I was tripping over the same import as it was also Euclidean geometry. What I ended up doing is extracting the core definition from the proof to its own file, and make its import list identical to the challenge file

And so to the broader question: is there somewhere I can read or learn about more of these sorts of subtle import issues?
I don't think so. These subtle import issues are pretty rare IME and usually easy to fix, as you can see what just happened here

(I started writing this before Yaël's message but I hope this still helps)

This happened because the statement involved a Fintype (Fin 2) instance, in order for the statement to be well-defined. You want that there is only one canonical instance to fill in a given hole, at all times, and this is a significant constraint on how instances are added to Mathlib.

When there are multiple instances, it can be somewhat nondeterministic which one gets picked in a given theorem statement, and this can cause issues. (so called "instance diamonds".) So multiple paths to an instance should be avoided ... with one major exception: if I have an instance inst1 : Foo A, and Bar extends Foo, and then later I build on inst1 to make inst2 : Bar A, then there's both inst1 and inst2.toFoo both available. But, since inst2 extends inst1, these are (after enough reduction) the same thing. Lean tactics and so on try to be robust to these issues where possible, understanding when two instances are actually the same.

Comparator works slightly differently and looks "into" terms differently, and has slightly different rules for how to tell when two instances are the same or not.

Really, this was a 'bug' in Mathlib, in the sense that there were two instances available that did not build in the proper way. Generally, you don't want that different imports want a theorem to "mean" something different, which is what happened here.
Ah sure, I meant "comparator-observable differences in instance behavior", but it's true that it's just instance diamond at the end of the day
